newsitem.title: USA: Tyson Foods lobbyist on trial in key case in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: Tyson Foods lobbyist on trial in key case in Espy probe.

text.p: The Washington lobbyist for mega chicken producer Tyson Foods goes on trial Monday for allegedly lying to federal investigators and legal experts said the outcome of the case will be key in the government's investigation of former Clinton cabinet member Mike Espy.

Jack Williams, chief lobbyist for the Arkansas-based poultry processor, has been charged with two criminal counts of making false statements to FBI investigators and other federal agents about his role in providing gifts to former Agriculture Secretary Espy on behalf of Tyson Foods.

The charges stem from an aggressive, two-year-plus investigation of Espy being led by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz. Espy has been accused of accepting illegal gratuities while a cabinet secretary from companies his agency regulated.

The investigation has resulted in criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns and sources close to the probe said that Espy, Tyson Foods and Don Tyson -- former head of the company and a longtime close friend of President Bill Clinton's -- are the key targets remaining in the case.
Whether Espy and Tyson will ultimately be criminally indicted may well be influenced by the outcome of the Williams trial, experts said.

"I think the Williams case, the outcome of this case, will probably be a factor in their continuing assessment into whether or not to bring charges against Don Tyson or Tyson Foods or Mr. Espy," said Washington attorney Thomas Green who represents the Tyson corporation.

The allegations against Espy - which led to his resignation in 1994 - first arose from reports that Espy had accepted football and airplane tickets from Tyson Foods, and that his girlfriend had improperly received an educational scholarship from the company.

The gifts were allegedly given in order to win preferential treatment from Espy in policies affecting the giant company, and were in violation of a longstanding federal law which specifically forbids any USDA officer or employee from accepting such gifts or favors.

The Smaltz team - after gaining some important guilty pleas and convictions in the investigation - is coming into the Williams trial fresh from a major setback in the related trial of Espy's brother Henry, who unsuccessfully ran for his brother's Mississippi congressional seat in 1993.
Henry Espy had been accused of conspiring to accept illegal campaign contributions, but the government's charges were dismissed by a Mississippi judge earlier this month.
Legal sources said that given the current critical stage of the investigation and the unexpected setback with Henry Espy, a successful outcome in the Williams trial is crucial.

"This trial may be the lynchpin in how people perceive them (the Smaltz team) from now on, and how they work with the investigation ... If the government loses this one, people could have the impression the investigation is crumbling," said attorney and former independent counsel Michael Zeldin.
The trial will showcase two top-notch attorneys.
Leading the government's case is Bob Ray, a former assistant U.S. attorney in Manhattan and an experienced criminal prosecutor.

Representing Williams is prominent Washington lawyer Henry Schuelke, whose clients have included White House secretary Carolyn Huber who found Hillary Clinton's Rose Law Firm billing records and Burt Lance, budget director under Jimmy Carter in the late 70's who was indicted for fraud. Schuelke helped Lance win acquittal on most counts and a hung jury on the rest in a five-month trial.
